title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter 26
paragraphs: Around four o'clock in the afternoon, Murat's troops began to enter Moscow. A detachment of Württemberg hussars rode in front, and behind them came the King of Naples himself with a large suite.
Midway along Arbat Street, near the Church of the Miraculous Icon of St. Nicholas, Murat halted. He was waiting for word from the advance detachment about the state of the citadel, le Kremlin.
A little crowd of the people who had stayed behind in Moscow gathered around Murat. They stared in timid bewilderment at this strange, long-haired commander decked out in feathers and gold.
"Is that their Tsar himself? Not bad!" low voices were saying.
An interpreter rode up to the group.

"Take off your cap... your caps!" The words passed from man to man through the crowd. The interpreter turned to an old porter and asked whether it was far to the Kremlin. The porter listened in perplexity to the unfamiliar Polish accent. He did not realize the man was speaking Russian, so he could not understand and slipped away behind the others.

Murat went up to the interpreter and told him to ask where the Russian army was. One of the Russians understood the question, and several voices at once began answering the interpreter. A French officer came back from the advance detachment, rode up to Murat and reported that the gates of the citadel had been barricaded, and that an ambush was probably waiting there.
"Good!" said Murat. He turned to one of the gentlemen of his suite and ordered four light guns brought forward to fire at the gates.

The guns came out at a trot from the column behind Murat and moved up the Arbat. At the end of Vozdvizhenka Street they halted and drew up on the Square. Several French officers supervised the placing of the guns and studied the Kremlin through field glasses.

In the Kremlin the bells were ringing for vespers, and the sound unsettled the French. They took it for a call to arms. A few infantrymen ran toward the Kutafyev Gate, where beams and wooden screens had been set up. As soon as an officer and his men started running to it, two musket shots rang out from under the gate. A general standing by the guns shouted a command to the officer, and the officer ran back with his men.
Three more shots came from the gate.

One shot hit a French soldier in the foot, and from behind the screens came the strange sound of a few voices shouting. All at once, as if at a word of command, the cheerful serenity on the faces of the French general, officers and men turned into a grim, concentrated readiness for struggle and suffering. For every one of them, from the marshal down to the humblest soldier, this place was not Vozdvizhenka, Mokhavaya or Kutafyev Street, nor the Troitsa Gate (all places familiar in Moscow), but a new battlefield, and probably a bloody one. And all of them got ready for that battle. The cries from the gate stopped. The guns were brought forward, the artillerymen blew the ash off their linstocks, and an officer gave the word, "Fire!" Two whistling sounds of canister followed, one after the other. The shot rattled against the stone of the gate and the wooden beams and screens, and two wavering clouds of smoke rose over the Square.

The echo of the reports had barely died away over the stone Kremlin when the French heard a strange noise above their heads. Thousands of crows rose over the walls and wheeled in the air, cawing and beating their wings noisily. With that noise came a solitary human cry from the gateway, and out of the smoke appeared a bareheaded man in a peasant's coat. He gripped a musket and aimed it at the French. "Fire!" the officer repeated, and a musket shot and two cannon shots sounded together. Smoke hid the gate again.

Nothing more moved behind the screens, and the French infantrymen and officers advanced to the gate. In the gateway lay three wounded men and four dead. Two others in peasant coats were running away along the foot of the wall, toward Znamenka.
"Clear that away!" said the officer, pointing to the beams and the corpses. The French soldiers finished off the wounded and threw the bodies over the parapet.

Nobody knew who these men were. "Clear that away!" was all anyone said of them, and they were thrown over the parapet and carried off later so they wouldn't stink. Thiers alone devotes a few eloquent lines to their memory: "These wretches had occupied the sacred citadel, having armed themselves from the arsenal, and fired" (the wretches) "on the French. Some of them were put to the sword, and the Kremlin was purged of their presence."

Murat was told that the way was clear. The French went in through the gates and began setting up camp in Senate Square. Soldiers threw chairs for fuel out of the windows of the Senate House into the Square and lit fires there.

Other detachments marched through the Kremlin and camped along Moroseyka, Lubyanka and Pokrovka Streets. Others took quarters along Vozdvizhenka, Nikolski and Tverskoy Streets. Nowhere did they find householders, so the French were not billeted on the inhabitants, as is usual in towns, but lived in the city as if in a camp.

The French were tattered, hungry, worn out and reduced to a third of their original number, yet they entered Moscow in good marching order. It was a weary and famished army, but still a fighting and menacing one. It stayed an army only until its soldiers had scattered to their separate lodgings. As soon as the men of the various regiments began to disperse among the rich, deserted houses, the army was lost forever. In its place came something indefinable, neither citizens nor soldiers but what are called marauders. Five weeks later, when these same men left Moscow, they were no longer an army. They were a mob of marauders, each carrying a load of things that seemed to him valuable or useful. When they left Moscow, each man's aim was no longer, as it had been, to conquer, but only to keep what he had got. A monkey puts its paw into the narrow neck of a jug, seizes a handful of nuts, and will not open its fist for fear of losing them, and so it perishes. The French were like that monkey. When they left Moscow they were bound to perish, because they were carrying their loot with them, and giving up what they had stolen was as impossible for them as it is for the monkey to open its paw and let go of the nuts. Ten minutes after each regiment entered a district of Moscow, not a soldier or officer was left. Through the windows you could see men in military uniforms and Hessian boots, laughing and walking through the rooms. In cellars and storerooms similar men were busy among the provisions. In the yards they were unlocking or breaking open coach house and stable doors, lighting fires in kitchens, kneading and baking bread with their sleeves rolled up, and cooking; or else frightening, amusing or caressing women and children. There were plenty of such men in the shops and houses — but there was no army.

That day the French commanders issued order after order. They forbade the men to scatter about the town, sternly forbade any violence to the inhabitants or any looting, and announced a roll call for that very evening. But despite all these measures, the men who until then had made up an army poured out over the rich, deserted city with its comforts and plentiful supplies. A hungry herd keeps well together while it crosses a barren field, but the moment it reaches rich pasture it gets out of hand and scatters uncontrollably. The army scattered over the wealthy city in just the same way.

There were no residents left in Moscow. The soldiers spread irresistibly in all directions from the Kremlin, where they had first marched in, like water seeping through sand. A cavalry unit would enter an abandoned merchant's house and find more than enough stabling for its horses, yet go on to the next house, which looked better to them. Many of them took over several houses, chalked their names on them, and quarreled and even fought with other companies over them. Before they had finished securing quarters, the soldiers ran out into the streets to see the city. Hearing that everything had been abandoned, they rushed to the places where valuables were there for the taking. The officers went after them to hold the soldiers back, and were drawn, against their will, into doing the same. In Carriage Row there were carriages left standing in the shops, and generals flocked there to pick out calèches and coaches for themselves. The few inhabitants who had stayed invited commanding officers into their houses, hoping to protect themselves from plunder that way. There was a mass of wealth, and it seemed to have no end. All around the quarters the French occupied lay other districts, still unexplored and unoccupied, where they thought even greater riches might be found. And Moscow swallowed the army deeper and deeper. When water is spilled on dry ground, both the dry ground and the water vanish and mud is left. In the same way, when the famished army entered the rich and deserted city, the result was fires and looting and the destruction of both the army and the wealthy city.

The French blamed the Fire of Moscow on au patriotisme féroce de Rostopchine, * and the Russians blamed it on the barbarity of the French. In reality, though, the burning of Moscow could not be explained by making any individual or any group of people responsible for it, and it never could have been. Moscow burned because it was in a position where any wooden town was bound to burn, whether or not it had a hundred and thirty poor fire engines. Deserted Moscow had to burn as surely as a heap of shavings burns when sparks keep falling on it for several days. A wooden town where hardly a day passes without a fire, even when the owners are at home and the police are present, cannot help burning once its inhabitants have left and soldiers occupy it — soldiers who smoke pipes, make campfires of the Senate chairs in Senate Square, and cook themselves meals twice a day. Even in peacetime, you only have to billet troops in the villages of a district and the number of fires there immediately goes up. How much more must the chance of fire increase in an abandoned wooden town with foreign troops quartered in it! "Le patriotisme féroce de Rostopchine" and the barbarity of the French were not to blame. Moscow was set on fire by the soldiers' pipes, kitchens and campfires, and by the carelessness of enemy soldiers living in houses that were not theirs. Suppose there was any arson (which is very doubtful, since nobody had any reason to burn the houses, a troublesome and dangerous thing to do in any case). Even so, arson cannot be counted as the cause, because the same thing would have happened without any incendiarism.
* To Rostopchin's ferocious patriotism.

It might be tempting for the French to blame Rostopchin's ferocity, for Russians to blame the scoundrel Bonaparte, or later to put a heroic torch into the hands of their own people. Still, one cannot help seeing that the fire could have had no such direct cause. Moscow had to burn as every village, factory or house must burn when its owners leave it and strangers are allowed to live in it and cook their porridge. Moscow was burned by its inhabitants, it is true, but by those who had abandoned it, not by those who stayed. Occupied by the enemy, Moscow did not remain intact like Berlin, Vienna and other towns, simply because its inhabitants abandoned it and did not welcome the French with bread and salt or bring them the keys of the city.
